lessons.title: AI and work: exposure is not a forecast
lessons.subtitle: What OECD and IAB numbers do not say

sections.title: Four terms, four different claims
sections.content:
Before you repeat the next number about threatened jobs: what does it measure? Studies do not all measure the same thing. Four terms, four claims:

1. Task exposure: a technology overlaps with an occupation's tasks. Nothing more.
2. Technical substitution potential: tasks could be automated with today's technology. Could.
3. Adoption: an employer introduces the technology and rebuilds the workflow.
4. Employment effect: working time, headcount, wages or skill requirements change.

Frey and Osborne estimated a theoretical automation probability for US occupations in 2013. The OECD Employment Outlook 2023 uses different data and methods, and reports the employment share in high-risk occupations across the OECD countries studied. That is no forecast for Germany. No prediction of specific job losses either.

The IAB uses BERUFENET to work out what share of an occupation's core tasks technology could in principle perform fully automatically. And the IAB says it plainly: substitutability does not mean the task gets automated.

Sources: OECD Employment Outlook 2023, Chapter 3; IAB Brief Report 5/2024 on the 2022 recalculation.
sections.keyTakeaway: Exposure, technical potential, adoption and employment effect are four different quantities. None alone tells you how many jobs disappear.

sections.title: Better than a human? At what exactly?
sections.content:
"AI is better than people." Better at what? Measured how? Without test conditions the sentence is worthless. Check four points:

- Task: are input, wanted output and quality measure defined?
- Data: do the test data match the real population and deployment?
- Consequences: what does an error cost, who reviews borderline cases?
- Environment: standardised, or physically and socially shifting?

A model can score high on a narrow image-classification test and be unfit for the clinic. A language model can speed up a draft and invent facts in the same paragraph. A planning system can handle every standard case and fail on one rare exception.

Legal responsibility, approvals and the weighing of interests sit with people and organisations. That says nothing about the model. It says who answers for the result.
sections.keyTakeaway: Judge a system against one task, one population, one error consequence. A benchmark proves no general superiority. Nor does fluency.

sections.title: One task becomes automatable. And the occupation?
sections.content:
An occupation is a bundle of tasks. When one becomes technically automatable, nothing about the occupation is decided. The employer can save time, handle more cases, redistribute work, raise quality or cut jobs. Demand, cost, liability, co-determination and new tasks pull in different directions.

Take radiology software that flags anomalies in images. Does it save the radiologist work, or add review? That turns on hit and error rates, the patient population, integration and oversight. A flag is not a diagnosis, let alone a treatment. Both stay medical work.

For your own job, a task analysis beats any forecast. Which steps are standardised? Where do errors arise? Which decisions need expertise, context or an approval? And where does the tool first create more checking?
sections.keyTakeaway: An automatable sub-task yields no occupational forecast. Technology, oversight and the remaining tasks decide, in the real workflow.

quiz.questionText: Which statement about labour-market studies on AI and automation is correct?

answerOptions.text: Every exposure figure directly forecasts future job losses
Exposure, technical potential and employment effect are different measures
The IAB measures only AI already in use in companies
The OECD Employment Outlook 2023 forecasts German unemployment caused by AI

quiz.explanation: Exposure and technical substitution potential describe where technology and tasks could overlap. Adoption and the employment effect turn on economic, legal and organisational factors.

quiz.questionText: What does the IAB substitution potential based on BERUFENET measure?

answerOptions.text: How many employees already use generative AI
Which occupations disappear within a year
What share of core tasks technology could in principle perform fully automatically
Which companies must automate by law

quiz.explanation: The IAB sorts core tasks by what technology could do at the time. That is technical potential. Not adoption, not viability, not job losses.

quiz.questionText: What follows from an automatable sub-task?

answerOptions.text: The whole occupation disappears within the next planning horizon
The technology is economical in every organisation
Every remaining task becomes more valuable to employees
The workflow can change; the employment effect has to be examined separately

quiz.explanation: Technical potential describes a task, nothing more. Whether that becomes time saved, extra review, higher case numbers or fewer positions, the deployment decides.

lessons.title: AI as assistance: measure, do not believe
lessons.subtitle: Who checks, who approves, which data go in

sections.title: Assistance without a performance promise
sections.content:
The vendor promises time saved. Your process has seen none. An assisted workflow gives the system one bounded step. Approval and accountability stay with a named person. Whether it saves time, you measure yourself.

Three synthetic examples, not case reports:
- A nurse drafts from approved, data-protection-compliant notes and checks every statement against the record. Patient data belong only in an approved system.
- An accountant has unusual entries flagged. The flag is a prompt to look. No fraud finding, no error finding.
- A communications team generates image drafts. Before publishing it checks rights, factual fit, disclosure and approval.

A controlled test fixes it in advance. Task, permitted data, quality criteria, who reviews, when to stop, what gets recorded. Only those measurements tell you whether it pays.
sections.keyTakeaway: Assistance is a workflow, not a performance promise. Bound the task, protect the data, review the results, measure the benefit.

sections.title: AI literacy: five abilities, no programming course
sections.content:
The case worker approving an AI draft needs no Python course. She needs five things.

1. Describe the task: purpose, context, format, limits.
2. Review the output: check claims, figures and sources against reliable material.
3. Recognise risk: with personal data, confidential information or consequential decisions, stop and escalate.
4. Place the tool: approval status, data handling, known limits, version changes.
5. Record the work: where the process demands it, trace inputs, outputs, changes, approvals.

Article 4 of the AI Act, as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, requires providers and deployers to take measures that support the development of AI literacy among their staff and others acting on their behalf. It does not demand a guaranteed level per person.
sections.keyTakeaway: AI literacy: place the task and the risk, protect the data, check the output, record the decision. No programming required.

sections.title: When the works council has a say
sections.content:
A tool counts how fast your colleague closes her tickets. May the employer decide that alone? Absent a statutory or collective-agreement rule, Section 87(1)(6) of the German Works Constitution Act (BetrVG) gives the works council co-determination over the introduction and use of technical equipment intended to monitor employees' behaviour or performance. Function and use decide whether an AI system falls under it. And the right sits with the works council, not with each employee.

Five questions that belong on the table:
- Which purpose, which decision does it support?
- Which employee data are collected, inferred or stored?
- Who sees the analyses, for how long?
- What oversight, correction and complaint route exists?
- What training and which binding rules apply?

If the two sides cannot agree in a co-determination matter, the conciliation committee decides under Section 87(2). That question is for qualified employment-law analysis, not this lesson.
sections.keyTakeaway: Section 87(1)(6) BetrVG can trigger works-council co-determination for monitoring AI. Purpose and function decide, not the label.

quiz.questionText: How do you recognise a controlled assistance workflow?

answerOptions.text: A fluent output counts as correct without further review
Task, permitted data, review and accountable approval are fixed in advance
Personal data may go into any available system
The benefit is taken from general vendor claims

quiz.explanation: A controlled workflow bounds the task, protects the data, sets quality criteria and hands review and approval to an accountable person. Gains in time or quality you prove in your own process, not from a brochure.

quiz.questionText: Which ability belongs to AI literacy if you have never programmed?

answerOptions.text: Training and calibrating your own models
Writing Python code for AI applications
Configuring and maintaining AI hardware
Assessing AI output critically and seeing its limits

quiz.explanation: Practical AI literacy: describe the task, check quality and sources, place the risk, know the tool, keep the work traceable. Programming can help. It is no prerequisite.

quiz.questionText: Which rule can bite for an AI system meant to monitor employee behaviour or performance?

answerOptions.text: Article 4 AI Act (measures supporting AI literacy)
Section 106 GewO (employer's right to issue instructions)
Article 22 GDPR (automated individual decisions)
Section 87(1)(6) BetrVG (co-determination for technical monitoring equipment)

quiz.explanation: Section 87(1)(6) BetrVG covers the introduction and use of technical equipment intended to monitor behaviour or performance. Whether its conditions are met turns on the system and its deployment.

lessons.title: Which tasks can change, and what you check yourself
lessons.subtitle: Task characteristics instead of occupation lists

sections.title: Repeated, digital, rule-based
sections.content:
The step repeats every day. The inputs are digital. Clear rules or a quality measure exist, and the setting barely changes. Then the technical potential runs high. Transferring structured data, checking formal completeness, drafting from a template.

Even then, adoption stays open. Bad data, rare exceptions, liability, integration cost or the checking afterwards can eat the benefit. The other way round, technology can support single steps in almost any job.

The IAB sorts core tasks against market-ready technology and refreshes that snapshot regularly. The unit of analysis is the task within the occupation. Not the occupation, certainly not its future.
sections.keyTakeaway: Standardised digital steps often carry higher technical potential. Automation is decided in the firm, nowhere else.

sections.title: What makes automation hard
sections.content:
The electrician stands on a site he has never seen. The nurse has patchy information and a relative in the room. There, automation gets hard. Harder still when a task combines several traits:

- a changing physical setting and fine-motor work
- incomplete information and rare exceptions
- direct responsibility for safety or fundamental rights
- negotiation among several parties
- relationship, trust or local knowledge

None of that makes an occupation "AI-proof". Documentation, planning and retrieval shift in care, trades, teaching and advice too. Robotics can move physical tasks over time. Look at tasks, not labels.
sections.keyTakeaway: Physical, social and legal context can make automation harder. No guarantee your job stays as it is.

sections.title: Three steps that get you further
sections.content:
No occupational forecast. Three steps.

1. Inventory your tasks: recurring steps, error consequences, data needed, approvals.
2. Test safely: approved tools only, test data only, nothing confidential or personal. Compare against a fixed reference.
3. Settle rights and responsibilities: Germany's Federal Employment Agency offers "Berufsberatung im Erwerbsleben", career guidance for people in employment, plus information on training and funding. In the firm: your manager, data protection, information security and, where relevant, the works council.

Article 5 of the AI Act has banned certain practices since 2 February 2025, among them emotion recognition at work, exceptions aside. Recruitment and selection systems can fall under Annex III. For stand-alone Annex III systems the high-risk rules start on 2 December 2027 under Regulation (EU) 2026/1744. The AGG, GDPR and employment law can apply independently, long before that.

If your hiring runs through such a system, ask five questions: what is it for? Which data does it use? What does the output mean? Where is the human? Who is accountable?
sections.keyTakeaway: Analyse the tasks, test inside the approved frame, settle who is responsible. Legal consequences turn on the specific system and its use.

quiz.questionText: Which task typically carries the higher technical automation potential?

answerOptions.text: A negotiation among several parties in a new conflict
A repair in an unfamiliar physical environment
A repeated formal completeness check on structured digital data
A consequential single-case judgement on incomplete information

quiz.explanation: Repeated digital steps that can be checked clearly often carry the higher technical potential. Whether the employer automates them is another matter.

quiz.questionText: What does Germany's Federal Employment Agency offer employees with training questions?

answerOptions.text: Automatic retraining for every occupation touched by AI
Career guidance for people in employment, with information on training and funding
A guarantee that every course you want gets funded
Mandatory certification under Article 4 of the AI Act

quiz.explanation: Germany's Federal Employment Agency offers career guidance for people in employment. What you get, whether a measure is fundable and who pays, turns on you, the measure and the rules in force.

quiz.questionText: Which statement about the EU AI Act at work is correct?

answerOptions.text: Article 5 prohibits every form of recruitment AI
All high-risk obligations have applied since 2 February 2025
Article 5 has nothing to do with the workplace
Article 5 has prohibited certain practices since 2 February 2025; recruitment AI must be assessed separately under Annex III and existing law

quiz.explanation: Article 5 has applied since 2 February 2025 to precisely named prohibitions, among them emotion recognition at work, exceptions aside. Recruitment and selection systems can fall under Annex III. The postponed high-risk dates you check separately, along with the AGG, GDPR and co-determination.
